Bishr narrated to me, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified﴾, he said: They will be terrified on the Day of Resurrection when they come out of their graves.

Qatadah said: ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape, and they will be seized from a near place﴾ refers to when they witness the punishment of God.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Ibn Ma'qil, regarding ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape﴾, he said: He will terrify them on the Day of Resurrection, so they will not escape.

The view most correct in the interpretation of this, and most consistent with what the apparent sense of the revelation indicates, is the view of those who said: It is the threat of God toward the polytheists who denied the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among his people. This is because the verses before this verse came with information about them and their causes, and with God's threat to them of its consequence, and this verse is in the context of those verses. So it is more fitting that this be information about their condition than that it be information about something that has not been mentioned. If that is so, then the meaning of the speech is: And if you could see, O Muhammad, these polytheists from your people, as you witness them when they are terrified at witnessing the punishment of God, ﴿but there will be no escape﴾, meaning: then there is no way at that time for them to escape by themselves, or to overpower us by fleeing and be saved from our punishment.

As:

Ali narrated to me, he said: Abu Salih narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape﴾, he said: meaning, there is no salvation.

'Amr ibn 'Abd al-Hamid narrated to us, he said: Marwan narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, but there will be no escape, and they will be seized from a near place﴾, he said: No flight.

And His saying ﴿and they will be seized from a near place﴾

Meaning: God will seize them with His punishment from a near place, because wherever they are, they are near to God and cannot be distant from Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 34, verse 52:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him." But how can they reach [faith] from a far place?﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: These polytheists, when they witnessed the punishment of God, said: "We have believed in Him," meaning: "We have believed in God and in His Book and His Messenger."

The interpreters of the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him"﴾: they said, "We have believed in God."

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him"﴾: "at that moment," meaning: when they witnessed the punishment of God.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him"﴾ [said] after being killed; and His words ﴿But how can they reach [it]﴾ he said: meaning, "From what direction can they reach it?"

The readers of the metropolitan cities differed concerning this. The majority of the readers of Medina recited ﴿al-tanawush﴾ without hamza, in the sense of "al-tanawul" (reaching/grasping). The majority of the readers of Kufa and Basra recited ﴿al-tana'ush﴾ with hamza, in the sense of "al-tana''ush," which is delay (al-ibta'); it is said of it: "tana'a'tu al-shay'": I took it from afar; and "na'asa-hu": I took it from near. From "al-tana'ush" is the verse of the poet:

*He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me, / and [yet] after matters have occurred, matters [have occurred].*

[[The lines are by Nahshal ibn Harri; Lisan al-'Arab cites them under (n-'-sh) with the hamzated form, meaning "he came late" (na'ish), i.e. slow. Ya'qub recited for Nahshal ibn Harri: "A client disobeyed me and took his own opinion alone, as Qasir's counsel was not obeyed. When he saw what came of my affair and his, and the fronts of matters turned their backs..." "He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me, and that matters would occur after matters." His saying "tamanna na'ishan" means at the end, and after the loss, that he had obeyed me, though matters have occurred that cannot be redressed. That is, he obeyed me at a time when obedience no longer benefited him. He said: it is also said, "he did it na'ishan," meaning late; and "he followed him na'ishan" when he lagged behind him and then followed him hastily, fearing that he would miss him. Al-na'ish also means distant, according to Tha'lab. Al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (Jami'a manuscript, folio 265): "And His words, '(and how can they reach the tanawush?)' al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with hamza, taking it from the slow thing, from na'asha, from al-na'ash." The poet said: "And you came late after the good had escaped you." Another said: "He wished for something..." to the end of the line. The people of the Hijaz and others omitted its hamza, taking it from nashahu nawshan, which is reaching; the two are close in meaning, like dammat al-shay' and dha'matuhu, meaning I blamed it. A poet said: "So she reaches the trough..." etc. "Tanawasha al-qawm fi al-qital" is said when some of them reached others in battle without coming fully close. Its hamza may also be permissible, and it is from nashat because of the wa' being pulled together, meaning al-tanawush, like His words: "And when the messengers are gathered (uqqitat)."]] From al-nawsh is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*So she reaches the trough with a reach from above, / a reach by which she cuts the wastes of the desert.*

[[These two lines are from the rajaz meter by Abu al-Najm the rajaz poet (Lisan: 'l-w). They are evidence that "min 'ala" means from above, from high up. There are other dialectal forms. Lisan also cites them under (n-w-sh), attributing them to Ghaylan ibn Hurayth, not Abu al-Najm, and takes them as evidence that the she-camel reaches the trough with her mouth, that is, she takes its water. He said: "min 'ala" means from above, meaning that her camels are tall of body and long of neck; that reach she makes is what helps us cross the wastelands. The "ajwaz" are the plural of "jawz," meaning the middle. That is, she reaches the water of the trough from above and drinks much, and by such drinking she crosses wastelands without needing other water. Abu 'Ubaydah cited it in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 200), attributing it to Ghaylan, and took it as evidence that the tanawush in the verse, for those who do not hamzate it from nashat yanush, means reaching. Ghaylan said: "So she reaches..." the two lines. Whoever hamzates it takes it from na'asha ilayhi, which is from distance. Lisan (n-'-sh) says: al-tana'ush with hamza means delay and distance; al-tanawush means taking from a distance, hamzated according to Tha'lab; he said: if it is from near, it is al-tana'ush. End of quote. I say: the two readings of Lisan agree with the reading of Abu 'Ubaydah, and they differ from the reading of the author in his saying "baata" in place of "fahiya."]]

It is said of people in war, when some of them come near the spears without meeting: "The people have tanawashu."

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that these are two well-known readings among the readers of the metropolitan cities, close in meaning. The meaning is: they said, "We have believed in God," at a time when such a saying will not benefit them. Then God said: ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾ That is, how can they have repentance and return? They have become far from it, so that it is like a distant place from which they cannot reach it. He described that place as distant because they said this on the Day of Resurrection, so God said: how can they have accepted repentance? Accepted repentance existed only in this world, and this world has gone, so it has become distant from the Hereafter. So whichever of the two readings you mentioned the reciter recites, he is correct in the truth.

It is possible that those who recited with hamza hamzated while meaning the sense of those who did not hamzate, but they hamzated it because of the wa' being pulled together, so they changed it, as is said: ﴿And when the messengers are appointed (uqqitat)﴾, where the wa' from waqqatat, when it is pulled, they hamzated it.

The interpreters said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said this:

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, saying: Isra'il related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Tamimi, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Tell me about the words of God: ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾" He said: "They ask for return, and it is not a time of return."

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from 'Anbasah, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Tamimi, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.

'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾: he says, "How can they have return?"

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, [concerning] ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾: "the return."

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, [concerning] ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾: he said: "the turning back" ﴿from a distant place﴾.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him. But how can they reach [it] from a distant place?"﴾: he said: "These are the slain of the people of Badr, those of them who were killed." And he recited ﴿And if you could but see when they are terrified, but there is no escape, and they are seized from a near place. And they say, "We have believed in Him"...﴾ the verse. He said: "al-tanawush" means reaching; "how can they reach repentance from a distant place," when they left it in the world. He said: "And this is after death, in the Hereafter."

He said: Ibn Zayd also said, concerning His words ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Him"﴾ [said] after being killed, ﴿But how can they reach [it] from a distant place?﴾ And he recited ﴿Nor of those who die while they are disbelievers﴾, and said: "They have no repentance." He said: God offered them that they repent once, and God would accept it from them, but they refused, or they offer repentance after death. He said: "They offer it in the Hereafter five times, and God refuses to accept it from them." He said: "The one who repents at death has no repentance." And [he recited] ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand over the Fire, and they say, "Oh, would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord..."﴾ the verse, and he recited ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us; we will do righteousness; indeed we are certain.﴾

'Amr ibn 'Abd al-Hamid related to us, saying: Marwan related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, concerning the words ﴿But how can they reach [it]?﴾: he said: "And how can they have return?"

* *

As for His words ﴿from a distant place﴾:

He says: from their Hereafter to the world.

As [it is related]:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿from a distant place﴾: from the Hereafter to the world.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 34, verse 53:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they had disbelieved in it before, and they hurl (accusations) at the unseen from a distant place﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying means: ﴿And they had disbelieved in it﴾, i.e., they disbelieved in what they asked their Lord (for) when the punishment descended upon them and they witnessed it, of reprieve from it, and that is faith in Allah, in Muhammad (ﷺ), and in what came to them from Allah.

And the interpretants (ahl al-ta'wil) have said what is similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And they had disbelieved in it before﴾: i.e., in faith in the world.

* *

And His saying ﴿and they hurl (accusations) at the unseen from a distant place﴾

It means: and they today hurl at Muhammad (ﷺ) from a distant place, meaning that they stone him, and (hurl at) what came to them of the Book of Allah with conjectures and delusions, so some of them say: he is a sorcerer, and some a poet, and other than that.

And the interpretants have said what is similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿and they hurl (accusations) at the unseen from a distant place﴾, he said: Their saying: a sorcerer; rather he is a soothsayer; rather he is a poet.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and they hurl (accusations) at the unseen from a distant place﴾: i.e., they stone with conjecture, saying: there is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Fire.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿and they hurl (accusations) at the unseen from a distant place﴾: with the Qur'an.

Tafsir of the verse: "And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before; indeed they were in disquieting doubt" (34:54). Translated from al-Tabari's Jami al-Bayan.

Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before; indeed they were in disquieting doubt﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: A barrier is placed between these polytheists, when they are terrified and there is no escape for them, and they are seized from a near place, and they say, "We believe in it" — ﴿and between what they desire﴾ at that time, of faith in what they used to disbelieve in during the world before that. And there is no way for them to reach it.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the scholars of interpretation) have said the like of what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Ismail ibn Hafs al-Ablli narrated to me, saying: Al-Mu'tamir narrated to us from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾: He said, "A barrier is placed between them and faith in Allah."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abd al-Samad, who said: I heard al-Hasan, when he was asked about this verse, ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾, say: "A barrier is placed between them and faith."

Ibn Abi Ziyad narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ashhab narrated to us, from al-Hasan: ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾, he said: "A barrier is placed between them and faith."

Ahmad ibn Abd al-Samad al-Ansari narrated to us, saying: Abu Usama narrated to us, from Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾, he said: "From returning to the world so that they might repent."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾. The people used to desire obedience to Allah, that they had acted upon it in the world, when they witnessed what they witnessed.

Al-Hasan ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ashhab narrated to us, from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾, he said: "A barrier is placed between them and faith."

Others said: The meaning of that is: a barrier is placed between them and what they desire of wealth, children and the splendour of worldly life.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾: He said, "Of wealth or children or splendour."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾: "In the world in which they were, and the life."

We have chosen the view we have chosen on this because the people only wished, when they witnessed the punishment of Allah that they witnessed, what Allah reported that they wished for, and said, "We believe in it." Then Allah said: ﴿And how can they reach it from a far place?﴾ and they had disbelieved before that in the world. If that is so, then His words ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾ being a report that there is no way for them to what they wished for is more appropriate than its being a report about something else.

* *

As for His words ﴿as was done with their counterparts before﴾:

He says: We have done this to these polytheists; We placed a barrier between them and what they desire of faith in Allah at the descent of Allah's wrath upon them and their witnessing of His might, just as We did to their counterparts, who disbelieved in Allah, among the disbelieving nations before them; so We did not accept their faith at that time, just as We did not accept it at a similar time from their peers.

Al-Ashya' (the counterparts) is the plural of shi', and shi' is the plural of shi'ah; so ashya' is the plural of a plural.

Ahl al-ta'wil have said the like of what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih: ﴿as was done with their counterparts before﴾, he said: "The disbelievers before them."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿as was done with their counterparts before﴾, i.e., in the world; when they witnessed the punishment, faith was not accepted from them.

* *

As for His words ﴿indeed they were in disquieting doubt﴾:

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: A barrier is placed between these polytheists, when they witness the might of Allah, and faith; indeed they were before, in the world, in doubt about the descent of the punishment that came upon them and that they witnessed. Their prophet had informed them that if they did not turn back from what they persisted in, of disbelief in Allah and worship of idols, Allah would destroy them and inflict His punishment upon them in the hasty part of the world and the deferred part of the Hereafter before its descent upon them. ﴿Disquieting (murib)﴾ means: causing its possessor what troubles him of harm, from the saying, "The man has made himself suspect (arab) when he commits an act of suspicion and commits a gross sin," as the rajaz poet said:

O people, what is wrong with me and Abu Dhu'ayb? Whenever I came to him from absence, he sniffs at my side and tears my garment, as if I had brought him suspicion with suspicion.

[Note: these verses are in rajaz, in the mashtur meter; they are cited by the author of Lisan al-Arab (under atay). He said: it is said "atawtuhu" (I came to him) is a dialectal form of "ataytuhu." Khalid ibn Zuhayr recited them. In another place he cited them under ريب and attributed them to Khalid ibn Zuhayr al-Hudhali, where the form is "ataytuhu" in place of "atawtuhu"; he used them as evidence that one says rabani amruhu, yuribuni, raybān and rayba, meaning "made me doubt"; and that arab, used intransitively, means "came with suspicion," as one says alam, meaning "came with what he is blamed for."]

He says: as if I had brought him a suspicion.

Here ends Surat Saba'.
